strengths: First systematic study of adversarial robustness of generative DNS (speech denoising/enhancement) models with imperceptibility constraints based on auditory masking, addressing an important and understudied gap given the widespread real-world deployment of these models.

Covers four diverse, recent, publicly available DNS architectures (Demucs, Full-SubNet+, FRCRN, MP-SENet) spanning time-domain and TF-domain approaches, and a broad set of experimental settings (varying SNR, presence/absence of reverb, over-the-air simulation), providing a fairly comprehensive robustness picture.

Goes beyond prior work (Dong et al.) by considering targeted attacks, more attack settings (near-zero noise, reverb, over-the-air), stronger imperceptibility constraints, and multiple evaluation metrics (STOI, ViSQOL, NISQA, DNSMOS, ASR WER), improving on the limitations of that closest related work.

Investigates multiple angles beyond the core attack: model transferability, universal adversarial perturbations, and a baseline Gaussian-noise defense, giving a more complete threat/defense picture rather than just a single positive result.

Interesting and non-obvious findings, such as the exploding-gradient pseudo-robustness of Full-SubNet+, the failure of naive attack transfer even between checkpoints of the same architecture, and the comparison suggesting audio DNS models are more fragile than analogous image denoising models.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (no human perceptual study/ABX test, reliance on white-box gradient access, discrete-token DNS models not covered, imperfect intelligibility metrics for targeted attacks) rather than overselling claims.
weaknesses: Central imperceptibility claims are not validated with a human listening/ABX study; the paper relies entirely on masking-threshold theory and metrics like STOI, which the authors themselves note can be misleading (e.g., their own targeted-attack STOI results are acknowledged to not correspond to perceptible target speech), undermining confidence in the 'imperceptible' framing throughout.

The targeted attack results are essentially inconclusive/negative in practice (authors admit only a 'faint robotic hint' of target speech is audible despite favorable STOI numbers), yet this is still framed somewhat positively in the abstract/intro ('near-term plausibility of targeted attacks'), which may overstate the actual achieved capability.

Threat model is limited to full white-box gradient access; no black-box/transfer-based or query-based attacks are demonstrated to succeed, and the negative transferability results (not even between checkpoints of the same architecture) somewhat weaken the practical real-world threat significance claimed in the introduction.

Evaluation is confined to simulated settings (simulated RIRs, simulated microphone/over-the-air conditions) rather than real physical over-the-air attacks, and the paper acknowledges the over-the-air perceptibility constraint had to be loosened (6 dB instead of 12 dB), introducing some audible artifacts and weakening the 'imperceptible' claim in that setting specifically.

The defense evaluation is very shallow, testing only Gaussian noise at various SNRs without any adaptive-attack evaluation against that defense, despite the paper itself noting (citing Tramer et al.) that adaptive attacks would likely defeat it—so the practical implications for defenders are limited.

Some methodological choices are under-justified or introduce confounds, e.g., inability to use PESQ due to licensing, reliance on STOI as both optimization objective and primary evaluation metric (potential circularity), and clipping audio to 5 seconds for MP-SENet due to VRAM limits, which could affect cross-model comparability.

Reproducibility could be stronger: hyperparameters and thresholds (e.g., the specific 12 dB/6 dB threshold shifts) appear somewhat ad hoc/tuned by the authors' own perception rather than a principled or validated procedure, and code availability is not explicitly confirmed in the visible text (only audio samples are mentioned as available online).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study across four diverse, recent open-source DNS architectures (time-domain and TF-domain) and a wide range of realistic conditions (SNR from 70dB to -10dB, reverb/no-reverb, simulated and real-recorded RIRs).

Careful, well-engineered perceptibility constraint: extends the standard MP3-style psychoacoustic masking model with temporal pre/post-masking and calibrated dB offsets, with an ablation (Appendix D.4) isolating the contribution of each component.

Strong empirical validation via a human study combining transcription (intelligibility) and ABX (imperceptibility) tasks, using principled two-way 'pigeonhole' bootstrap statistics appropriate for crossed participant/item designs, plus an intersection-union test for the main intelligibility claim.
Use of multiple complementary objective metrics (STOI, ViSQOL, NISQA, DNSMOS, ASR WER) rather than relying on a single metric, improving robustness of the evaluation.

Commendable scientific honesty: the paper reports several negative/mixed results (failure of naive model transfer, ineffectiveness of universal perturbations, subjective failure of targeted attacks despite metric success) rather than overselling positive findings.

Extensive appendices with sanity checks (fixed-iteration comparison, real RIR validation, leave-one-out transfer, perceptibility-tradeoff sweeps) that substantially strengthen confidence in the main claims and rule out several confounds.

Good positioning relative to prior work (Dong et al.), explicitly identifying and addressing three key gaps (imperceptibility rigor, targeted attacks, real-world condition coverage), and detailed licensing/reproducibility documentation for all external assets.
weaknesses: Core technical contribution is largely an application/extension of existing techniques (psychoacoustic hiding from Schönherr/Qin et al., PGD) to a new target domain (DNS) rather than a fundamentally new attack methodology, which somewhat limits novelty.

The practical threat is substantially narrowed by the paper's own negative results: attacks require white-box gradient access, do not transfer across architectures or even checkpoints of the same architecture, and imperceptible universal perturbations do not work — meaning the attacker essentially needs full model access and per-utterance optimization, which is a much weaker threat model than implied by the alarming framing in the abstract/intro.

Targeted attacks, one of the paper's stated contributions, are shown to be subjectively unconvincing despite favorable objective metrics, undermining the significance of that finding beyond a cautionary note about metric reliability.

The human study, while methodologically careful, is small (15 participants, all from a single industrial lab, non-blinded to being lab colleagues of the potential authors) and the key ABX imperceptibility result is only marginally above chance and not statistically significant (lower bound 0.478), leaving genuine ambiguity about true imperceptibility.

Reliance on STOI as both attack objective and primary evaluation metric raises some circularity/validity concerns, even though the authors partially address this with auxiliary metrics and human studies; PESQ, a standard intelligibility metric, could not be used due to licensing.

Over-the-air experiments required loosening the masking threshold offset (6dB vs. 12dB) to achieve success, which somewhat weakens the paper's central imperceptibility claims in the most realistic (OTA) setting.

Only the simplest possible defense (Gaussian noise) is evaluated, with no adaptive-attack-aware defense tested, despite the paper itself citing evidence that such simple defenses are easily circumvented by adaptive attackers — leaving the practical security implications somewhat open-ended.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental design covering four DNS models, multiple SNR/reverb conditions, five computational metrics, simulated and real-RIR over-the-air attacks, and multiple ablations (perceptibility constraint sweep, fixed-iteration sanity check, attack-pipeline component ablation) — this breadth strengthens confidence in the core untargeted-attack result.

Honest and detailed reporting of negative/mixed results (targeted attacks succeed by STOI but not subjectively, UAPs largely fail, cross-model/cross-checkpoint transfer fails, Gaussian noise defense only partially effective) rather than only showcasing successes, which is good scientific practice.

Careful statistical methodology for the human study (two-way 'pigeonhole' bootstrap CIs appropriate for crossed participant/item design, intersection-union test for the primary intelligibility claim), which is more rigorous than typical ad hoc significance testing in this literature.

Clear, well-motivated positioning relative to the closest prior work (Dong et al. 2023), explicitly identifying and addressing three specific gaps (imperceptibility rigor, targeted vs. untargeted attacks, real-world condition coverage).

Mechanistic insight that FullSubNet+'s apparent robustness stems from exploding/obfuscated gradients rather than genuine robustness is a useful and non-obvious finding with implications for how robustness should be evaluated.
weaknesses: Core methodological contribution is largely an application of existing techniques (MP3/Qin et al.-style psychoacoustic masking combined with standard PGD) to a new target domain (DNS models) rather than a fundamentally new attack or defense technique; the main novelty is empirical/application-level rather than methodological.

The human study, which is central to substantiating the paper's imperceptibility claims, is small (n=15) and drawn entirely from a single industrial research lab with no external compensation or independent recruitment, raising concerns about participant motivation/bias and generalizability; the paper itself acknowledges no formal IRB review was sought.

The ABX imperceptibility result (59% accuracy) is not statistically significant relative to chance, which is reported as 'preliminary support' but in fact represents a fairly weak empirical basis for the paper's headline imperceptibility claim — this is a meaningful gap between the claimed contribution and the evidence.

Full-SubNet+ was excluded from the human study specifically (described as focusing budget on 'most vulnerable' models), which is a reasonable practical choice but reduces the completeness of the paper's central human-validated claims across all four studied models.

PESQ, a standard and widely recognized intelligibility metric, could not be used due to licensing constraints, leaving a gap relative to established evaluation practice in the field despite the paper's use of several substitute metrics.

The practical threat model is somewhat overstated relative to what is demonstrated: attacks require white-box gradient access, are per-utterance and offline (not streaming), and naive transfer fails entirely, meaning the realistic severity of the threat to deployed black-box systems remains largely speculative despite the paper's rhetorical framing around safety-critical applications (hearing aids, ATC radio, emergency response).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study spanning four state-of-the-art open-source DNS models, multiple SNR/reverb conditions, and simulated over-the-air (including real recorded RIR) settings, going well beyond the scope of the only prior work on this topic (Dong et al.).

Rigorous human evaluation (transcription + ABX studies with domain experts) that validates both the unintelligibility of attacked outputs and the imperceptibility of the perturbations, using an appropriate crossed-effects (pigeonhole) bootstrap methodology and an intersection-union test for the primary claim, rather than relying solely on proxy metrics.

Careful, well-justified psychoacoustic masking pipeline with temporal pre/post-masking and threshold offsets, with an ablation (Appendix D.4) isolating the contribution of each pipeline component and quantifying the perceptibility-vs-success tradeoff.

Honest reporting of negative/mixed results (failed universal perturbations, weak model transfer, targeted attacks that succeed by objective metrics but not subjectively), which strengthens the credibility and scientific value of the paper rather than overselling the threat.

Useful mechanistic insight that Full-SubNet+'s apparent robustness stems from obfuscated/exploding gradients rather than genuine architectural robustness, correctly contextualized against the obfuscated-gradients literature.
Extensive supplementary experiments (fixed-iteration sanity check, defense evaluation, real RIR validation, license/reproducibility documentation) that support reproducibility and rule out confounds.
weaknesses: The core technique (STFT-domain psychoacoustic masking + PGD) is largely adapted from existing ASR adversarial attack literature (Qin et al., Schönherr et al.); the paper's novelty lies primarily in application/extensiveness rather than new methodology.

The threat model is strictly white-box with full gradient access; naive black-box transfer fails, which somewhat limits the practical urgency of the claimed security threat despite the authors' argument that open-source models make gradients available.

The human study is small (15 participants from a single industrial lab, non-independent expert pool) and the ABX imperceptibility result (59% accuracy) is not statistically significant, with substantial variance—this is acknowledged but weakens the central imperceptibility claim.
PESQ, a standard and widely trusted intelligibility metric, could not be used due to licensing restrictions, leaving a gap relative to prior literature's typical evaluation protocol.

Targeted attacks, one of the paper's stated contributions relative to Dong et al., are shown to largely fail subjectively despite favorable STOI values, undermining the claimed advance in attack goals.

Over-the-air experiments, while validated with real recorded RIRs, still do not account for real playback-chain nonlinearities, automatic gain control, or codec compression, which the authors themselves note could attenuate the attack in fully realistic deployments.
